judges.rationale: Both reports are dense and well-sourced with timestamped claims, but Report A's Key Facts, Analysis, and Conclusions sections almost entirely omit two full transcripts (DeepLoop Circle/Vivek and Absent Data) despite listing them in its stats table, leaving real coverage gaps. Report B treats all 11 videos substantively, including precise verifiable numbers (penguin species counts, weekday sales totals, tips correlations) explicitly marked as 'also visible on screen,' and even flags a genuine speech/visual discrepancy (grid lines claimed but not shown), demonstrating more careful and correct visual evidence use. Neither report shows clear misattribution of screen content as speech or fabricated claims. B's broader, more granular, and better visually-grounded coverage makes it the stronger source per minute of reading.

Both reports provide dense, accurate summaries of the provided transcripts with high detail. Report A stands out slightly for its exceptional use of visual spans, explicitly cross-referencing on-screen data with spoken claims (e.g., noting a discrepancy between the speaker's claim of a grid and its absence on screen, and pulling specific numerical values from visual frames to supplement the analysis). Report A extracts slightly more detailed analytical takeaways.

on: This report synthesises 11 videos (11 transcripts, 55,389 words, 226 minutes of runtime) from 10 distinct channels covering matplotlib and seaborn data visualization instruction in Python.

Publication dates run from 2018-11-22 to 2026-09-28, with a median of 2025-04-13; by year the corpus breaks down as 3 videos in 2026, 3 in 2025, 2 in 2023, 2 in 2022 and 1 in 2018, with all 11 videos carrying a date.

The evidence base for these findings comprises 178 key facts, 39 analytical observations, 21 conclusions, 19 historical and external references, and 13 attributed speaker contributions, drawn from the 11 transcripts described above.

The source item for this consolidated summary is attributed to a Simplilearn presenter but is timestamped within the Data Analytics Lab video; readers should treat the attribution of the summarising voice as uncertain while the four findings themselves are corroborated by the individual segments above.
Of the thirteen source items, only two carry a personal name for the speaker, and one item is not a speaker at all but an automated on-screen annotation layer.

The same holds for the second half of the CodeWithMunnaX Seaborn material, where the instructor remains unidentified through the 14:13–27:22 stretch of Seaborn in Python | Introduction to Seaborn | Data Visualization Tutorial for Beginners — CodeWithMunnaX (14:13).
The video was published on 2018-11-22, so the figures were roughly current at publication; readers should treat them as a snapshot of the 2014–2018 window and not as indicative of later prices.
off: Where sources disagree, the disagreement tracks publication date and should be read that way.

The single 2018 video and the 2022–2023 cohort reflect older seaborn idioms — notably sns.distplot() and sns.set_style() — which the 2025 and 2026 videos replace with histplot/displot and set_theme(), reflecting seaborn's deprecations and the v0.11/v0.12 API shift.

Chart coverage clusters tightly. Line, bar, scatter, histogram and pie charts dominate the matplotlib segments; seaborn segments concentrate on countplot, boxplot, violinplot, heatmap (especially correlation matrices), pairplot, distplot/histplot and the figure-level relplot/catplot family.

Shorter, exam-oriented treatments — Gate Smashers at 1,973 words over 9 minutes, Onur Baltaci at 1,817 words over 12 minutes — compress the material to definitions and a handful of plot types, while the longer builds from DeepLoop Circle (5,751 words, 29 minutes), Academind (5,464 words, 27 minutes) and Data Analytics Lab (9,661 words across 2 videos, 47 minutes) spend their time on customisation, subplots, real datasets and interpretation of the resulting charts.
Readers choosing a learning path should match the format to the goal: the short videos answer "what is seaborn?", the long ones answer "how do I make this figure publication-ready?"

In the demonstrated two-row, two-column arrangement, Microsoft price is displayed in the lower-right subplot and Apple price in the lower-left subplot after specifying the appropriate row and column indices — Academind (26:26).
Second, he characterizes newly created subplots as "raw templates" because they do not yet contain data (15:17), a framing that treats the figure/axes object as scaffolding rather than output.
The following are not stated by any single video; they emerge from reading the twelve items together.
The corpus for this report consists of eight tutorial videos drawn from seven YouTube channels.
A structural feature of the material deserves to be stated up front: none of the transcripts identifies its presenter by personal name.
Across all nine source items the speaker field resolves to an unnamed instructor.
For NeuralNine, Gate Smashers, CodeWithMunnaX and Academind the source material notes explicitly that "no personal name is provided in the transcript."
At roughly 27 minutes this is the longest single item in the corpus, and the curricular numbering signals an intent to build cumulatively rather than deliver a standalone overview.

judges.rationale: A is much denser in transcript-verifiable specifics: datasets, code calls, parameter names, numeric values, chart interpretations, and timestamps. It also uses visual-only evidence carefully, usually labelling it as visible/on screen. A has some unsupported metadata and source-count claims. B is more concise but loses substance and has serious unsupported chronology/API-shift claims, wrong corpus/source counts in Speaker Contributions, and at least one incorrect visual/layout claim. Per minute of reading, A gives a researcher more verified facts despite padding and some fabricated metadata.
